question: How can three different ideas belong to one sonata argument?
intro: A slow introduction prepares a movement with three distinguishable thematic ideas. The main fanfare becomes a memory carried through the symphony; here, follow its replies, the contrasting themes and their transposed returns.

cues.title: A slow beginning
cues.text: Dvořák starts with an Adagio before the main Allegro molto. The introduction already anticipates material used later, so its hesitant phrases belong to the movement’s thematic argument.

cues.title: Lower strings begin the sentence
cues.text: The opening foreground is in the violas and cellos, with other instruments entering around them. Listen to the low melodic line rather than expecting a violin-led introduction.

cues.title: Pauses give phrases edges
cues.text: The introduction separates gestures with rests and changes of texture. A pause can make the next phrase feel like a reply without introducing a new melody.

cues.title: A call and its response
cues.text: The Allegro’s main theme contains a fanfare-like opening and a contrasting response. Its announcing gesture will recur in later movements, linking the symphony through memory.

cues.title: Written in New York
cues.text: Dvořák composed the symphony between 10 January and 24 May 1893 during his first year in the United States. It was complete before his summer visit to Spillville, Iowa.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Rhythm marks the identity
cues.text: Dotted rhythms and displaced accents help identify the principal material. Keep a rhythmic profile in mind when an idea moves to another instrumental group.

cues.title: A more restricted range
cues.text: The second subject begins with a narrower melodic compass and a lowered seventh. Its later transformation changes the character without discarding the underlying idea.

cues.title: Burleigh’s singing mattered
cues.text: The African American singer Harry T. Burleigh sang spirituals for Dvořák in New York. The connection is documented; it does not make every pentatonic melody in the symphony a quotation.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Three supporting ideas
cues.text: The exposition contains a main subject, a contrasting second subject and a lyrical closing theme. Hear their differences in phrase shape and rhythmic emphasis rather than forcing the movement into two tunes only.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Pressure across the development
cues.text: This central span sustains considerably more recorded force than the quiet end of the exposition. Follow the succession of gestures through the changing harmonic ground.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: The level rises from about −26 dB at 5:10 to −8 dB at 6:00, with further strong windows at 6:10–6:20.

cues.title: Development changes the harmony
cues.text: The development recombines earlier ideas while moving through several key regions. Repetition of a short shape can create continuity across a rapidly changing harmonic background.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A conservatory in America
cues.text: Dvořák was directing New York’s National Conservatory when he wrote the symphony. His American stay placed him in direct contact with musicians whose repertories differed from those he had known in Prague.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: A return, with transposition
cues.text: The recapitulation closely follows the exposition, but the secondary and closing themes return a semitone higher. Recognisable material need not return at its original pitch level.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The first theme looks ahead
cues.text: The fanfare-like main subject matters beyond this movement. Keep its contour in memory for later appearances in the Largo, scherzo and finale.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

cues.title: Seidl conducted the premiere
cues.text: Anton Seidl conducted the New York Philharmonic Society’s premiere at Carnegie Hall on 16 December 1893. A public rehearsal the previous afternoon had already attracted a large audience.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: The closing weight persists
cues.text: The last stretch maintains a strong recorded level across several phrases. It does not retreat immediately after the coda’s first crest.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: Windows from 9:10 through 9:55 stay relatively strong, including high levels at 9:25, 9:30 and 9:50.

transitions.title: The introduction releases the Allegro
transitions.how: The Adagio’s separated gestures prepare the main theme rather than forming a detachable prelude. A B-dominant preparation leads into the Allegro’s E-minor call and response, with quicker articulation and clearer rhythmic direction.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: The 1:55 window is quiet, with B prominent; level and attack activity rise at 2:00 as the score’s E-minor Allegro begins. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The fanfare makes room
transitions.how: The forceful main-subject region relaxes into a more restricted melodic line. The second subject’s lowered seventh and narrower compass distinguish it from the opening call while retaining rhythmic links with the larger argument.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: Level falls from the 2:30 crest towards 3:00; the 3:04 boundary marks renewed activity within the quieter second-subject region. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: A third idea closes the exposition
transitions.how: The second-subject region gives way to a more lyrical closing melody. Its pentatonic outline and longer phrases supply another kind of contrast before the development, rather than merely decorating the first subject.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: The 4:20–4:25 windows are exceptionally quiet before the rising 4:30–4:50 span; the G-major destination is established by the score, with chroma as corroboration. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: Stable themes enter changing harmony
transitions.how: The exposition’s close is followed by development of the earlier ideas. Sequential movement through changing keys makes short recognisable shapes do work outside their original settings.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: A strong boundary at 5:12 follows the closing-theme decline; level and attack activity then rise across 5:20–6:10. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The main call returns
transitions.how: The developmental motion gives way to the main subject again. The return restores E minor, but the recapitulation does not keep every later theme at its exposition pitch.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: The 6:26 reduction is followed by a strong boundary at 6:38 and renewed E-minor-compatible activity at 6:45–6:55. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: A familiar contrast is transposed
transitions.how: The main-subject return again relaxes into the secondary material. Dvořák places this region a semitone above its earlier setting, so thematic recognition and tonal placement do not coincide exactly.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: Level falls towards 7:20; the ensuing 7:25–7:45 pitch profile supports the score’s transposed secondary region. Chroma is not the sole identification. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The closing theme returns higher
transitions.how: The lyrical closing idea follows the secondary material as before, now also a semitone higher. Its phrase shape remains recognisable despite the changed tonal location.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: A quiet 8:35 window precedes the rise through 8:40–9:00; the score establishes the closing theme’s A♭-major return. Written design: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/ Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The main subject claims the ending
transitions.how: The coda redirects the lyrical close to the movement’s main material and E-minor destination. Brass and timpani reinforce the fanfare rather than introduce another independent theme.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/dvorak-9-adagio.txt: The 9:10 boundary is also the report’s loudest window; the remaining span sustains stronger levels and E-minor-compatible pitch content before the final decay. source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, full score, critical edition edited by Otakar Šourek
source.locator: First movement: printed pp. 1–72 (PDF pp. 3–74). The short piccolo phrase is in bars 197–200, printed p. 34 (PDF p. 36); no tuba is scored in this movement. Time positions remain broad passage estimates.

timeline.note: Introduction region: violas and cellos begin the line; wind and horn responses enter around the low strings.
The introduction’s forceful wind, horn and string gestures include timpani (printed p. 3, PDF p. 5). Broadly anchored to the report’s strong 1:00–1:05 rise, not an exact drum entrance.
The introduction reduces to wind figures, horn replies and quieter strings (printed p. 4). The report’s 1:14 boundary and quiet 1:15–1:20 windows anchor the change of scale.
Later introductory gestures add trumpets and trombones to winds and strings (printed p. 5). Broad placement follows the report’s 1:36 boundary and renewed stronger gestures before the Allegro.
Main-subject region: horn call and string response develop into fuller orchestral statements.
Main-subject climax: trombones and timpani reinforce the full wind, brass and string scoring (printed p. 11, PDF p. 13). The 2:30 window is one of the report’s strongest.
Secondary region: wind-led melodic statements and string support replace the opening fanfare’s weight.
Closing-theme region: the flute’s lyrical line expands into broader wind and string statements.
Development region: earlier figures pass between strings, winds and brass through changing harmonies.

The development’s brief piccolo phrase lies over quiet strings, with the horn’s tail and a trumpet continuation (bars 197–200, printed p. 34). Approximately placed in the report’s 5:20–5:25 E-major region, not bar-aligned.
After the piccolo’s short phrase, wind and trumpet exchanges continue over strings; the second flautist returns to flute (printed p. 34). Broadly placed before the 5:30 change.
The central development regains fuller wind, brass and timpani reinforcement as the report rises through 5:40–6:20. Tuba is not part of this movement.
Recapitulation region: the main subject returns, followed by lighter secondary and closing-theme scoring.
Secondary return: the strings prepare a quiet bed for the solo flute’s transposed melody (printed pp. 52–53). The 7:15–7:30 reduction anchors this lighter region, not the flute’s first note.
The secondary material expands through wind and string doubling, with horn and trombone reinforcement (printed p. 58). Broad placement follows the 7:56 boundary and the stronger 8:00 window.
The expanded secondary return thins to wind phrases and strings (printed p. 62), matching the recorded withdrawal across 8:25–8:35 before the closing theme.

Closing-theme return: solo flute over quieter strings, followed by oboe, clarinet and bassoon support (printed p. 63). This broad state starts with the 8:40–8:55 rise, not the previous brass-led main subject.
Coda region: brass and timpani strengthen the main subject and E-minor cadence.

composer.epithet: A theatre violist who made dance accents, remembered songs and classical development work inside the same movement.
facts: Local teachers in Bohemia; Prague Organ School, 1857–59
Violist in Prague’s Provisional Theatre orchestra, 1862–71; organist and private teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York, 1892–95
Nine symphonies, operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs; B numbers refer to Jarmil Burghauser’s catalogue
composer.background:
Dvořák was born in Nelahozeves, a village north of Prague, where his father kept an inn and worked as a butcher. He learnt violin locally and acquired further musical training at Zlonice before attending the Prague Organ School in 1857–59. He earned his living in ensembles, including the orchestra of Prague’s Provisional Theatre from 1862 to 1871, playing viola under conductors who included Smetana. Opera taught him how a middle part supports singers, how repeated figures sustain a scene and how instrumental colour carries across a crowded theatre.

His early compositions were extensive and often ambitious: chamber music, symphonies and operatic projects accumulated before he had a dependable publisher. Wagner’s influence is audible in the scale and harmonic movement of some of these works. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková. Teaching and an organist’s post helped support the household while applications for an Austrian state stipend brought his scores to influential readers. The award first received in 1875 brought both honour and money at a point when publication and commissions remained uncertain.
